This document discusses the ongoing antitrust trial against Google, focusing on the company's practices and defenses. Key points include Google's payments to secure default search engine status, attempts to preinstall Google services on Apple devices, and the deletion of internal chat logs. The case highlights the struggle between Google's dominance and the need for fair competition.

Google antitrust trial, Eddy Cue, Apple's Senior Vice President of Internet Software & Services, testified about the Information Services Agreement (ISA) with Google, which makes Google the default search engine on Apple devices. The deal has been in place since 2002, and Apple negotiated a higher revenue share with Google in 2016. During his testimony, Cue emphasized that Apple believed in Google's product quality and prioritized user privacy, stating there was no viable alternative to Google at the time.

Cue was on the stand as a witness in US v. Google, the landmark antitrust trial over Google’s search business. Cue is one of the highest-profile witnesses in the case so far, in part because the deal between Google and Apple — which makes Google the default search engine on all Apple devices and pays Apple billions of dollars a year — is central to the US Department of Justice’s case against Google.

Apple is in court because of something called the Information Services Agreement, or ISA: a deal that makes Google’s search engine the default on Apple’s products. The ISA has been in place since 2002, but Cue was responsible for negotiating its current iteration with Google CEO Sundar Pichai in 2016. In testimony today, the Justice Department grilled Cue about the specifics of the deal.
